items.stem: Which research method best describes the study by Piliavin, Rodin and Piliavin (1969) on helping on the New York subway?
options: field experiment
laboratory experiment
semi-structured interview
covert participant observation
items.answer: field experiment
items.markingKey: A. Piliavin, Rodin and Piliavin (1969): On the New York subway, a confederate "victim" carrying a cane (ill) or smelling of alcohol (drunk) collapsed in a carriage; covert observers recorded who helped and how quickly over about 4,450 passengers.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Controlled observations have higher ecological validity than naturalistic observations.
Reason (R): Controlled observations take place in settings designed by the researcher.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
items.answer: A is false but R is true.
items.markingKey: D. A is false - controlled settings are more artificial; R is true.

items.stem: A student claims: "Observations can show the cause of behaviour." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Observations record what happens but do not manipulate an IV, so they cannot establish causality on their own.
items.markingKey: Observations record what happens but do not manipulate an IV, so they cannot establish causality on their own. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe observing children's play at break time and explain what it reveals about overt naturalistic observation.
items.answer: Two IB students in Geneva observe how many children play in mixed-gender groups during break time, sitting on a bench with notebooks. Behaviour is natural, but children may notice the students and change behaviour (reactivity); public setting reduces consent issues but parents and the school should agree
items.markingKey: Context (Two IB students in Geneva observe how many children play in mixed-gender groups during break time, sitting on a bench with notebooks.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: behaviour is natural, but children may notice the students and change behaviour (reactivity); public setting reduces consent issues but parents and the school should agree – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to overt naturalistic observation.

items.stem: A student wants to observe whether people hold doors open for others at a shopping centre in Kuala Lumpur. Recommend a type of observation and justify it.
items.answer: Covert, non-participant naturalistic observation: people's helping behaviour is natural if they do not know they are observed; acceptable ethically as it is a public place where people expect to be seen, with no identifying data recorded.
items.markingKey: Covert, non-participant naturalistic observation: people's helping behaviour is natural if they do not know they are observed; acceptable ethically as it is a public place where people expect to be seen, with no identifying data recorded.

items.stem: Evaluate Whyte (1943).
items.answer: Strengths: rich, long-term insider data; key informant gave access and checked interpretations. Limitations: researcher became involved (e.g. voting several times in an election) - loss of objectivity; one neighbourhood; hard to replicate.
items.markingKey: Strengths: rich, long-term insider data; key informant gave access and checked interpretations. Limitations: researcher became involved (e.g. voting several times in an election) - loss of objectivity; one neighbourhood; hard to replicate. Award marks for points explicitly applied to this study (generic points score at most 1). items.stem: Define the term "structured observation".
items.answer: An observation that uses predetermined behaviour categories and a systematic sampling method
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an observation that uses predetermined behaviour categories and a systematic sampling method. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain what the study by Piliavin, Rodin and Piliavin (1969) suggests about helping behaviour in a naturalistic setting.
items.answer: Findings: the "ill" victim received spontaneous help on 95% of trials and the "drunk" victim on about 50%; there was no diffusion of responsibility in this setting. Link: these results are evidence about helping behaviour in a naturalistic setting.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for accurate findings (the "ill" victim received spontaneous help on 95% of trials and the "drunk" victim on about 50%; there was no diffusion of responsibility in this setting); remaining marks for explicitly explaining what the findings show about helping behaviour in a naturalistic setting (not just restating them).

items.stem: Using Whyte (1943) as supporting evidence, explain participant observation of a social group.
items.answer: Whyte (1943). Aim: to understand the social structure of an Italian-American neighbourhood and its street-corner gangs. Method: Whyte lived for about three years in the North End of Boston ("Cornerville"), joining the "Norton Street gang" with the help of its leader "Doc", who knew he was a researcher; he kept detailed field notes. Findings: he found a highly organised social structure with clear hierarchies and obligations, challenging the view that slums were disorganised Link: participant observation of a social group.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: he found a highly organised social structure with clear hierarchies and obligations, challenging the view that slums were disorganised); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to participant observation of a social group. A study that is described but not linked cannot score more than half marks.

items.stem: With reference to the six concepts of the course, discuss the claim that covert observation is the best way to study real behaviour.
items.answer: Covert observation gives the most natural data in public settings, but ethical limits mean overt or controlled observation is often preferable.
items.markingKey: For: avoids reactivity (Hawthorne effect); natural behaviour - high ecological validity. Against: no informed consent; privacy concerns; cannot ask participants about motives; harder to record reliably. Supported conclusion: Covert observation gives the most natural data in public settings, but ethical limits mean overt or controlled observation is often preferable. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A precise description of an observable behaviour so that observers can identify it consistently"?
options: non-participant observation
limitation (of a study)
operational definition (observation)
blind observer
items.answer: operational definition (observation)
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of operational definition (observation).

items.stem: Rafael writes: "High inter-rater reliability means the observation is valid." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Observers can agree consistently and still measure the wrong thing (e.g. a poorly chosen category); reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity.
items.markingKey: Observers can agree consistently and still measure the wrong thing (e.g. a poorly chosen category); reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between time sampling and event sampling.
items.answer: Time sampling records behaviour at set intervals (good for frequent behaviour, may miss brief events); event sampling records every occurrence of a target behaviour (good for infrequent events, harder when behaviour is frequent).
items.markingKey: Time sampling records behaviour at set intervals (good for frequent behaviour, may miss brief events); event sampling records every occurrence of a target behaviour (good for infrequent events, harder when behaviour is frequent). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Ana recorded the following frequencies: helped = 51; did not help = 48; helped after a delay = 54. Calculate the percentage of the total that was "helped after a delay" (to 1 decimal place) and identify the modal category.
items.answer: 35.3%; modal category: helped after a delay
items.markingKey: A1 54/153 x 100 = 35.3%. A1 mode = helped after a delay (54).

items.stem:
Elena and Zara used time sampling to code pedestrians at a crossing every 30 seconds (W = waits for signal, J = crosses against signal, P = uses phone while crossing).
Elena: W J P W P P J P W W
Zara: P J P W P P J W W W

Calculate the percentage agreement between the two observers and explain whether inter-rater reliability is acceptable.
items.answer: 8/10 intervals agree = 80.0%; acceptable (the usual benchmark is 80%).
items.markingKey: M1 agreements counted: 8 of 10. A1 8/10 x 100 = 80.0%. R1 ≥ 80%, so reliability is acceptable.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Structured observations with behaviour checklists provide reliable data."
items.answer: Checklists increase reliability, but researchers must pilot and refine categories and check agreement during the observation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: clear categories enable high inter-rater agreement; quantitative data can be analysed. Arguments against: categories may miss important behaviour; observer bias and drift over time; reliability does not guarantee validity. Supported judgement: Checklists increase reliability, but researchers must pilot and refine categories and check agreement during the observation.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "percentage agreement"?
options: A measure of inter-rater reliability: the number of agreements divided by the total number of observations, multiplied by 100
A change in behaviour that occurs because people know they are being observed (participant reactivity)
The right of people not to have their personal lives observed without permission, especially in non-public places
A place where people would expect to be seen by strangers, where observation without consent may be acceptable
items.answer: A measure of inter-rater reliability: the number of agreements divided by the total number of observations, multiplied by 100
items.markingKey: A. "percentage agreement" is a measure of inter-rater reliability: the number of agreements divided by the total number of observations, multiplied by 100.

items.stem: Explain how inter-rater reliability can be improved.
items.answer: Train observers together using example videos, refine ambiguous categories, use a pilot observation, and calculate agreement until it reaches an acceptable level (e.g. 80%).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Train observers together using example videos, refine ambiguous categories, use a pilot observation, and calculate agreement until it reaches an acceptable level (e.g. 80%). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Design a behaviour checklist with four categories for observing helping behaviour in a school canteen. Give an operational definition for each.
items.answer: E.g. holding a door (keeps door open for another person for 2+ seconds); picking up a dropped item for someone; offering to share food or a seat; giving directions/help when asked - categories observable and mutually exclusive.
items.markingKey: E.g. holding a door (keeps door open for another person for 2+ seconds); picking up a dropped item for someone; offering to share food or a seat; giving directions/help when asked - categories observable and mutually exclusive.

items.stem: State the aim of the study by Rosenthal and Fode (1963) on experimenter expectancy with rats.
items.answer: Aim: to investigate whether experimenters' expectations influence the results they record. Method: Psychology students were each given rats to train in a maze; half were told their rats were "maze-bright" and half "maze-dull", although the rats were randomly assigned.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for an accurate aim (to investigate whether experimenters' expectations influence the results they record); 1 mark for an accurate method or design (psychology students were each given rats to train in a maze; half were told their rats were "maze-bright" and half "maze-dull", although the rats were randomly assigned.)

items.stem: "Using video recordings removes all ethical issues in observation." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Video increases accuracy but raises additional issues of consent, data storage and identifiability.
items.markingKey: Video increases accuracy but raises additional issues of consent, data storage and identifiability. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why observers should not know the hypothesis of a study.
items.answer: Knowing the hypothesis can lead them, consciously or not, to notice and record behaviour that supports it (observer/expectancy bias); blind observers record more objectively. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Knowing the hypothesis can lead them, consciously or not, to notice and record behaviour that supports it (observer/expectancy bias); blind observers record more objectively. items.stem: Briefly describe a long observation session and explain what it reveals about observer drift and fatigue.
items.answer: Two observers in Oslo code playground aggression for 90 minutes without a break; by the end they are recording fewer pushes than at the start for similar behaviour. Tiredness and gradual changes in applying definitions reduce reliability; shorter sessions, breaks and re-checking agreement would help
items.markingKey: Context (Two observers in Oslo code playground aggression for 90 minutes without a break; by the end they are recording fewer pushes than at the start for similar behaviour.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: tiredness and gradual changes in applying definitions reduce reliability; shorter sessions, breaks and re-checking agreement would help – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to observer drift and fatigue.

items.stem: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in Rosenthal and Fode (1963), and explain how the dependent variable was operationalised.
items.answer: IV: expectation given to the student (maze-bright vs maze-dull). DV: recorded number of correct maze runs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark IV (expectation given to the student (maze-bright vs maze-dull)); 1 mark DV (recorded number of correct maze runs); 1 mark for an appropriate operationalisation or a relevant extraneous variable (e.g. participant variables, demand characteristics, order effects) with a brief justification.

items.stem: Evaluate Rosenthal and Fode (1963).
items.answer: Strengths: random assignment of labels isolates the effect of expectations. Limitations: students may have handled rats differently (a real effect) or recorded results inaccurately - mechanism unclear; deception of student experimenters.
items.markingKey: Strengths: random assignment of labels isolates the effect of expectations. items.stem: Briefly explain why observer bias is a problem in observational research.
items.answer: Observers may see what they expect - e.g. interpreting rough play as aggression in boys more than girls - so data reflect the observer's expectations rather than the behaviour.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Observers may see what they expect - e.g. interpreting rough play as aggression in boys more than girls - so data reflect the observer's expectations rather than the behaviour. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A researcher observing a religious ceremony is a member of that faith. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of this for the observation.
items.answer: Advantage: understands meanings and is accepted (insider perspective, access); disadvantage: may take behaviour for granted or interpret it in line with own beliefs (bias), and may find it hard to report negative findings.
items.markingKey: Advantage: understands meanings and is accepted (insider perspective, access); disadvantage: may take behaviour for granted or interpret it in line with own beliefs (bias), and may find it hard to report negative findings.

items.stem: "Observer bias makes observational research unscientific." Discuss.
items.answer: Observer bias is a real threat, but it can be reduced to an acceptable level by careful design.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: expectations affect recording; interpretation of behaviour is subjective. Arguments against: operational definitions and blind observers reduce bias; inter-rater reliability checks; bias exists in all methods. Supported judgement: Observer bias is a real threat, but it can be reduced to an acceptable level by careful design. items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Experiments are the most useful class practical for understanding behaviour."
items.answer: Each practical answers different kinds of questions; experiments are best for causality, but combining methods gives the fullest understanding.

items.stem: Suggest how a researcher could protect participants' confidentiality when observing patients' behaviour in a hospital waiting room.
items.answer: Gain permission from the hospital ethics board; record behaviour categories only, without names or descriptions that identify people; store notes securely; report results as group data; display a notice about the research.
items.markingKey: Gain permission from the hospital ethics board; record behaviour categories only, without names or descriptions that identify people; store notes securely; report results as group data; display a notice about the research.

items.stem: Using an unseen study on music and exercise as an example, explain evaluating an unseen study.
items.answer: An unseen study reports that 20 gym members in Toronto ran longer with fast music than slow music; members chose which session to attend. Self-selection to conditions confounds the IV (motivated runners may choose fast music); the gym sample limits generalisability; random allocation and counterbalancing would improve validity
items.markingKey: Context (An unseen study reports that 20 gym members in Toronto ran longer with fast music than slow music; members chose which session to attend.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: self-selection to conditions confounds the IV (motivated runners may choose fast music); the gym sample limits generalisability; random allocation and counterbalancing would improve validity – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to evaluating an unseen study.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Covert observation is the best way to study real behaviour."
items.answer: Covert observation gives the most natural data in public settings, but ethical limits mean overt or controlled observation is often preferable.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: avoids reactivity (Hawthorne effect); natural behaviour - high ecological validity. Arguments against: no informed consent; privacy concerns; cannot ask participants about motives; harder to record reliably. Supported judgement: Covert observation gives the most natural data in public settings, but ethical limits mean overt or controlled observation is often preferable.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Structured observations with behaviour checklists provide reliable data."
items.answer: Checklists increase reliability, but researchers must pilot and refine categories and check agreement during the observation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: clear categories enable high inter-rater agreement; quantitative data can be analysed. Arguments against: categories may miss important behaviour; observer bias and drift over time; reliability does not guarantee validity. Supported judgement: Checklists increase reliability, but researchers must pilot and refine categories and check agreement during the observation. items.stem: Using two relevant studies, discuss the claim that observer bias makes observational research unscientific.
items.answer: Observer bias is a real threat, but it can be reduced to an acceptable level by careful design.
items.markingKey: For: expectations affect recording; interpretation of behaviour is subjective. Against: operational definitions and blind observers reduce bias; inter-rater reliability checks; bias exists in all methods. Supported conclusion: Observer bias is a real threat, but it can be reduced to an acceptable level by careful design. items.stem: Which of the following was the aim of the study by Piliavin, Rodin and Piliavin (1969) on helping on the New York subway?
options: To understand the social structure of an Italian-American neighbourhood and its street-corner gangs
To investigate whether stereotype threat affects the performance of Black students on verbal tests
To investigate the effect of the victim's condition (drunk or ill) and race on helping behaviour in a natural setting
To investigate whether experimenters' expectations influence the results they record
items.answer: To investigate the effect of the victim's condition (drunk or ill) and race on helping behaviour in a natural setting
items.markingKey: C. Piliavin, Rodin and Piliavin (1969) aimed to investigate the effect of the victim's condition (drunk or ill) and race on helping behaviour in a natural setting.

items.stem: Recording what a child is doing every 15 seconds is an example of:
options: Event sampling
Random sampling
Time sampling
Snowball sampling
items.answer: Time sampling
items.markingKey: C. Behaviour is recorded at fixed intervals.

items.stem: Which strategy reduces observer bias?
options: Telling observers the expected results
Making the categories vaguer
Using observers who are blind to the hypothesis
Using only one observer
items.answer: Using observers who are blind to the hypothesis
items.markingKey: C. Blind observers cannot record selectively to support the hypothesis.

items.stem: "Evaluating a study means only listing its weaknesses." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Evaluation weighs strengths and limitations and judges how much they affect the conclusions.
items.markingKey: Evaluation weighs strengths and limitations and judges how much they affect the conclusions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline the findings of Whyte (1943) and explain one conclusion about participant observation of a social group that can be drawn from them.
items.answer: Findings: he found a highly organised social structure with clear hierarchies and obligations, challenging the view that slums were disorganised. Link: these results are evidence about participant observation of a social group.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for accurate findings (he found a highly organised social structure with clear hierarchies and obligations, challenging the view that slums were disorganised); remaining marks for explicitly explaining what the findings show about participant observation of a social group (not just restating them).

items.stem: Briefly explain why behaviour categories must be operationally defined.
items.answer: Clear, observable and mutually exclusive definitions mean different observers record the same behaviour in the same way, increasing inter-rater reliability and reducing observer bias.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Clear, observable and mutually exclusive definitions mean different observers record the same behaviour in the same way, increasing inter-rater reliability and reducing observer bias. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between observer bias and participant reactivity.
items.answer: Observer bias comes from the observer's expectations affecting what is recorded; participant reactivity is a change in participants' behaviour because they know they are being observed.
items.markingKey: Observer bias comes from the observer's expectations affecting what is recorded; participant reactivity is a change in participants' behaviour because they know they are being observed. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a limitation of an unseen study and a strength of an unseen study.
items.answer: A strength is a feature that increases confidence in the conclusions (e.g. random allocation); a limitation is a feature that reduces it (e.g. a self-selected sample); both must be linked to the study's claims.
items.markingKey: A strength is a feature that increases confidence in the conclusions (e.g. random allocation); a limitation is a feature that reduces it (e.g. a self-selected sample); both must be linked to the study's claims. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how the findings of Piliavin, Rodin and Piliavin (1969) provide evidence about helping behaviour in a naturalistic setting.
items.answer: Findings: the "ill" victim received spontaneous help on 95% of trials and the "drunk" victim on about 50%; there was no diffusion of responsibility in this setting. Link: these results are evidence about helping behaviour in a naturalistic setting.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for accurate findings (the "ill" victim received spontaneous help on 95% of trials and the "drunk" victim on about 50%; there was no diffusion of responsibility in this setting); remaining marks for explicitly explaining what the findings show about helping behaviour in a naturalistic setting (not just restating them).

items.stem: A student claims: "High inter-rater reliability means the observation is valid." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Observers can agree consistently and still measure the wrong thing (e.g. a poorly chosen category); reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity.
items.markingKey: Observers can agree consistently and still measure the wrong thing (e.g. a poorly chosen category); reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Using video recordings removes all ethical issues in observation." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Video increases accuracy but raises additional issues of consent, data storage and identifiability.
items.markingKey: Video increases accuracy but raises additional issues of consent, data storage and identifiability. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A researcher in Dubai measures heart rate of participants who are told they will give a speech in 5 minutes compared with participants told they will read silently. Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable.
items.answer: IV: expectation of giving a speech vs reading silently. DV: heart rate in beats per minute.
items.markingKey: 1 mark IV: expectation of giving a speech vs reading silently. 1 mark DV: heart rate in beats per minute (must be operationalised, not just named).

items.stem: With reference to Piliavin, Rodin and Piliavin (1969), explain how research has investigated helping behaviour in a naturalistic setting.
items.answer: Piliavin, Rodin and Piliavin (1969). Aim: to investigate the effect of the victim's condition (drunk or ill) and race on helping behaviour in a natural setting. Method: On the New York subway, a confederate "victim" carrying a cane (ill) or smelling of alcohol (drunk) collapsed in a carriage; covert observers recorded who helped and how quickly over about 4,450 passengers. Findings: the "ill" victim received spontaneous help on 95% of trials and the "drunk" victim on about 50%; there was no diffusion of responsibility in this setting Link: helping behaviour in a naturalistic setting.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: the "ill" victim received spontaneous help on 95% of trials and the "drunk" victim on about 50%; there was no diffusion of responsibility in this setting); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to helping behaviour in a naturalistic setting. A study that is described but not linked cannot score more than half marks.

items.stem:
Sana and Hana used time sampling to code pedestrians at a crossing every 30 seconds (W = waits for signal, J = crosses against signal, P = uses phone while crossing).
Sana: J P W P W W P J W J W W
Hana: J P W W W W P J W J W P

Calculate the percentage agreement between the two observers and explain whether inter-rater reliability is acceptable.
items.answer: 10/12 intervals agree = 83.3%; acceptable (the usual benchmark is 80%).
items.markingKey: M1 agreements counted: 10 of 12. A1 10/12 x 100 = 83.3%. R1 ≥ 80%, so reliability is acceptable.

items.stem: Describe the study by Rosenthal and Fode (1963) and explain what it shows about observer and experimenter expectancy bias.
items.answer: Rosenthal and Fode (1963). Aim: to investigate whether experimenters' expectations influence the results they record. Method: Psychology students were each given rats to train in a maze; half were told their rats were "maze-bright" and half "maze-dull", although the rats were randomly assigned. Findings: rats labelled "maze-bright" were recorded as learning the maze faster, showing that experimenters' expectations biased the results Link: observer and experimenter expectancy bias.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: rats labelled "maze-bright" were recorded as learning the maze faster, showing that experimenters' expectations biased the results); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to observer and experimenter expectancy bias. A study that is described but not linked cannot score more than half marks.

items.stem: A psychology student, Mei, collected the following data on scores on a 30-item vocabulary test: 8, 11, 8, 14, 11, 9, 10, 8, 30. Calculate the mean (to 2 decimal places) and the median, and explain which is the more appropriate measure of central tendency for these data.
items.answer: Mean = 12.11; median = 10; more appropriate: the median, because the extreme score of 30 inflates the mean.
items.markingKey: A1 mean = 109/9 = 12.11. A1 median = 10 (ordered: 8, 8, 8, 9, 10, 11, 11, 14, 30). R2: the median, because the extreme score of 30 inflates the mean.

items.stem: Evaluate Piliavin, Rodin and Piliavin (1969).
items.answer: Strengths: high ecological validity - real passengers; large opportunity sample. Limitations: no informed consent or debriefing; passengers may have been distressed; observers' recording may be inaccurate in a crowded carriage.
items.markingKey: Strengths: high ecological validity - real passengers; large opportunity sample.
